1.sense: An oath by the sky, and then by something that arrives in it after dark. The thing sworn by is named for the sound it makes on arrival rather than for what it is, and the surah will spend two more verses telling you what it means.

notes.t: Tariq comes from tarq, to strike or knock. An Arab called a night visitor a tariq because anyone arriving after dark had to knock at the door to be let in, and the word carries that unannounced arrival up into the sky.
The surah asks what the tariq is in the next verse and answers in the one after, so it defines its own oath before it uses it. Very little else in the Qur'an is built this way.
Jabir ibn Samurah reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah and its like in the noon and afternoon prayers, so it had a place in his ordinary week rather than only in his night.

links.why: the surah immediately before opens with an oath by the sky
another surah that swears a chain of oaths before naming what they establish

2.sense: The question is put to the Prophet ﷺ himself. It is not decoration. The Qur'an uses this formula when it is about to supply something the hearer could not have reasoned his way to, and it pauses first so he notices that he did not have it.

notes.t: The exegetes keep two formulas apart. Where the Qur'an asks wa ma yudrika, what will make you know, the answer is withheld and the matter stays with Allah. Where it asks wa ma adraka, what has made you know, an answer follows immediately. This is the second kind, and verse three delivers it.

The verb adra is the causative of dara, to know by picking something up. It asks not whether you know but what could possibly have told you, which rules out the sky, experience and inheritance in one word.
The same construction opens the Qur'an's own account of the Night of Decree and of the Striking Calamity, both times on a thing no observer could have measured.

links.why: the same question asked of the Night of Decree, then answered
the same formula opening onto the Striking Calamity

3.sense: The answer is two words. Thaqib is what a drill does to wood: it goes all the way through. The star is identified by its light getting through the dark, not by its size, its name or its place in the sky.

notes.t: Which star is meant was never settled. Reports from the early generations name a particular planet, and others read an-najm as the whole kind rather than one of them, which is ordinary Arabic usage.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the reports naming a single star and those reading the genus, and decides for neither

notes.t: Thaqib is from th-q-b, to bore a hole. The Arabs used it of a lamp turned up until it burns white. The word is about penetration, so the oath is by light that does not merely shine but gets in.
The Qur'an uses the same adjective of the flame that pursues a devil trying to eavesdrop on the heavens, which keeps the star in the register of something that goes after what it is aimed at.

links.why: the same word thaqib, there of a piercing flame
the nearest heaven set with lamps that double as missiles

4.sense: This is what the oath was sworn to establish. Not most souls and not the ones that matter to somebody. Every soul, and the sentence is built as a negation with an exception so that no reader can quietly place himself outside it.

notes.t: Two canonical readings stand here. Hafs, the reading of this Mushaf, has lamma with the doubled meem, which makes in a negation and lamma mean except. A lightened lama is transmitted from other readers, which makes in affirmative and the lam emphatic. The sentence says the same thing either way.
notes.src: Hafs reads lammā; a lightened lamā is transmitted from Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr

notes.t: Hafiz is one who keeps a thing from being lost. It is the same word used of a person who has committed the Qur'an to memory. What a hafiz does, in every use of the word, is not lose what was given to him.
The Qur'an identifies the guardians elsewhere as recording angels, noble and writing, so the keeper here is not an abstraction or a conscience.

links.why: the guardians named plainly, noble ones who write
angels before him and behind him, guarding by the command of Allah

5.sense: A command to look, and the thing to be looked at is not the sky the surah has just sworn by. It is the reader's own beginning. The argument turns from the far and impressive to the near and slightly embarrassing.

notes.t: Khuliqa is passive, he was created, which leaves the maker unnamed for three more verses. The grammar makes the reader supply Him before the text does.
The command is in the third person, let the human being look, rather than look. Arabic uses this to state a duty that stands whether or not the person addressed accepts it.
The Qur'an points this same instruction at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth and the self. The evidence it keeps asking for is never in a book.

links.why: and in yourselves, so will you not see
the same command to look, there aimed at the camel

6.sense: The answer to the question the verse before asked. It is deliberately plain and slightly undignified, because the whole argument depends on the reader admitting how little he started out as.

notes.t: Dafiq is grammatically active, gushing, although the fluid is what gets poured rather than what pours. Arabic allows the active form where the sense is passive, and the exegetes read it as poured out under force.
The noun is indefinite, a fluid, not the fluid. Nothing about it is singled out or dignified, and that is the point of the sentence rather than an accident of it.
The Qur'an describes the same origin elsewhere in blunter terms still, calling it a fluid held in contempt.

links.why: did We not create you from a fluid disdained
the same beginning, there set out in stages

7.sense: The fluid is given a place of departure, named by two parts of the body. What exactly those two parts are, and whose body they belong to, is where the commentaries part company and have stayed parted.

notes.t: The identification is old and unresolved. Some read both parts as the man's, the backbone and the front of his chest. Others read the sulb as the man's and the tara'ib as the woman's, which makes the verse describe the two parents together.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both identifications from the early generations without preferring one

notes.t: Tara'ib is a plural with no clean English equivalent. The lexicographers place it at the upper chest, the area where a necklace lies, between the collarbones and the breast.
The verse names a place of exit, not a mechanism. Reading a modern account of embryology into it, whether to defend it or to attack it, presses it for an answer to a question it is not putting.

links.why: posterity made from an extract of a fluid held cheap
the stages of the making set out in order

8.sense: The conclusion the last three verses were built to carry. The One who assembled a person out of that can reassemble him, and the verse puts it as a question of capacity rather than of promise, because capacity was what the deniers were disputing.

notes.t: What the returning refers to is discussed. Most read it of bringing the person back to life after death. A minority read it as returning him to the state he came from, which keeps the argument to the same body.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, and the majority of the exegetes take it of the resurrection

notes.t: Qadir is the participle of one who has the power now, not one who will acquire it when the time comes. The lam in front of it is the lam of emphasis, so the sentence is an assertion twice over.
The Qur'an puts the identical argument as an objection and answers it: who will give life to bones after they have crumbled, and the reply names the One who made them the first time.

links.why: the same argument raised as an objection and then answered
He begins the creation and repeats it, and repeating is easier

9.sense: The Day is named by what happens to hidden things, not by the sky splitting or the mountains moving. Tubla is the verb for putting a thing under trial in order to find out what it actually is, and here the thing tested is the inside of a person.

notes.t: Sara'ir is the plural of sarira, from the root s-r-r, what a person keeps to himself. It covers intentions and not only concealed deeds, so what is examined is the reason behind the record rather than the record.

Bala is the same verb the Qur'an uses of Allah testing people in this life with good and with harm. Applying it to the secrets makes the last event an assay rather than a sentence: the result is a finding about what a thing was.
The Qur'an states the same outcome without the metaphor: that Day you will be exhibited, and nothing of you stays concealed.

links.why: and what is in the breasts is brought out and collected
you are exposed, and nothing hidden of you stays hidden

10.sense: Two supports are removed in one line: what a person can do for himself, and what anyone else can do for him. The order runs from the inside outward, and nothing is left standing behind it.

notes.t: The particle min before quwwatin makes the denial total in Arabic. It is not that he has little strength on that Day. He has none of the category at all.
The pronoun is singular and unattached. The verse does not say the denier or the criminal, only him, so no reader has yet been told he is outside the sentence.
The Qur'an describes the same Day as one on which no soul holds anything at all for another soul, which is the second half of this verse stated as a general rule.

links.why: no soul possesses anything for another soul that Day
no relative avails a relative, and they are not helped

11.sense: A second oath opens the second half of the surah, and the sky is sworn by again, this time under a description rather than by name alone. It is the sky that gives back what it took up.

notes.t: What the return names is not agreed. The commonest reading is the rain, which the Arabs themselves called the return because it comes back season after season. Others read it of the sun, moon and stars returning to their places.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the rain and the returning heavenly bodies, and the exegetes divide between them

notes.t: Raj is the same root as raji in verse eight, where Allah is said to be able to return a human being. The sky giving its water back and the Maker giving His creature back are put under one word, so the second half of the surah rests on the first.
The oath is by a habit rather than by an object. What is sworn by is not the sky but a thing the sky reliably does, which is the sort of evidence a farmer already trusts.

links.why: We poured the water down in abundance, said without an oath
the same construction, an oath by the sky under a description

12.sense: The matching oath from below. Sad is a crack in something solid, and the earth is sworn by as the thing that opens. What comes up through the crack is left unsaid, because everyone who has watched a field knows it.

notes.t: Sad is used of a crack in glass or in rock. Applied to soil it names the split a seedling makes on its way up, which is a small violence that nobody ever notices happening.
Sky above and earth below, one giving back and one opening. The two oaths take in the whole visible world between them, and both of them describe one event from its two ends.
The Qur'an spells the pair out without oaths in another place: the water poured down, and then the earth split open.

links.why: then We split the earth open, a splitting
a dead land brought back to life, and such is the coming out

13.sense: The thing both oaths were sworn to. Fasl is the word for cutting one thing away from another, so a qawl fasl is a statement that separates. After it there is a right side and a wrong side where before there had been discussion.

notes.t: Fasl is the root behind the word for a judge's ruling and the word for a season of the year, both of them things that divide. The Qur'an calls the Day of Judgement yawm al-fasl on exactly the same logic.
What the pronoun refers to is discussed. Most exegetes read it of the Qur'an, since the surah has been contested speech from the start. Some read it of the resurrection announced in verse eight.
notes.src: at-Tabari prefers the Qur'an; the reading of the resurrection is also recorded

notes.t: The Qur'an describes itself elsewhere as a Book of unassailable standing, one that falsehood cannot get at from in front or behind.

links.why: the Day of Decision, named from the same root
the Book described as one falsehood cannot approach

14.sense: The denial that follows the claim. Hazl is speech said for amusement, the kind the speaker does not stand behind. The verse rules the Qur'an out of that category, which means every sentence in it is meant to be acted on.

notes.t: Hazl is the standing opposite of jidd, seriousness, in ordinary Arabic. The pairing was already worn smooth by use, and the verse picks the harder of the two and attaches it to the Book.
The denial has an audience. In Makkah the recitation was being treated as material to laugh at between other business, and the verse names that response before refusing it.
The Qur'an describes the same crowd elsewhere as listening while they play, and as amusing themselves at the moment the warning arrives.

links.why: and you are amusing yourselves while this is being recited
no reminder reaches them but they listen to it while they play

15.sense: The subject changes without warning from the Book to the people arranging themselves against it. Kayd is planning done quietly, with the target not meant to find out until it is finished.

notes.t: The verb and its object come from one root, yakiduna kaydan. In Arabic that doubling intensifies rather than repeats: they are not making a plan, they are plotting hard at it.
The tense is present and continuous. This is not a plot that was made once and recorded; it is being made while the verse is being recited, which is why the reply in the next line is also present.
The Qur'an sets out what the plotting of Makkah actually consisted of: to confine the Prophet ﷺ, or kill him, or drive him out.

links.why: the plot of Makkah set out in its three options
they schemed a scheme and We schemed a scheme

16.sense: The reply uses their own verb back at them, and it is said in the first person singular, which the Qur'an keeps for moments when nothing at all stands between the speaker and the matter.

notes.t: This is muqabala, answering a word with the same word. The Qur'an does it with mockery, deception and plotting alike, and it does not mean Allah does what they do. It means their act is met on its own ground and outmatched there.
Theirs is plural and His is singular, and the singular is the one that settles the matter. The asymmetry is the whole argument of the line.
The Qur'an states the same exchange with the outcome attached: they schemed and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers.

links.why: I give them time; indeed My plan is firm, both halves in one line
they schemed and Allah schemed, and He is the best of schemers

17.sense: The instruction that closes the surah is not a counterattack. Having just been told that the plotting is already answered from above, the Prophet ﷺ is told to do nothing about it and wait, and the waiting is handed to him with a short measure attached.

notes.t: Two verbs from one root sit side by side, mahhil and amhil, one intensive and one plain. Saying it twice in two forms is how Arabic settles a matter the hearer might otherwise argue with.
Ruwaydan is a diminutive of a word that already means a little. It shortens the wait twice over, so the command is patience with an end fixed to it in advance rather than patience without limit.
The same instruction is given in another Makkan surah with the same verb: leave Me and the deniers, and grant them a little respite.

links.why: leave Me and the deniers, and grant them respite a little
We let them enjoy a little, then drive them to a heavy punishment
